Despite the promising advances in the field of 2PIC for data centers, significant gaps remain in the literature. Particularly, few studies have comprehensively addressed the application of these fluids in 2PIC systems. Recent work by Pottker et al. [17] introduced a new developmental dielectric fluid, Opteon™ 2P50, detailing its properties and dielectric characteristics. Still, the performance evaluation of 2P50 in actual systems under a wide range of operating conditions deserves further exploration. This study sought to assess the performance of Opteon™ 2P50, in a commercially available 2PIC system across a wide range of thermal loads and ambient conditions, to assess the performance in different climate zones. In addition, a semiempirical lumped model of the 2PIC system was developed, validated with experimental data, and used for parametric studies to explore potential performance enhancements. The results are anticipated to provide meaningful insights and support the adoption of sustainable 2PIC cooling technologies in data centers. 2 3. EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY The section includes a description of the 2PIC tank, dielectric fluid, test matrix, experimental procedure, and data reduction, including the uncertainty analysis. 3.1 2PIC SYSTEM DESCRIPTION The liquid tank shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2 is designed for two-phase immersion cooling. This tank has a rated cooling capacity of up to 6.0 kW. This tank can house up to four “U” servers up to 533 mm wide and 1,000 mm deep within the main tank. Each U server is 44.5 mm deep. The external system dimensions are 965 × 723 × 1774 mm. Power input requirements are met with two 200–240 V, 50~60 Hz, single-phase connections using NEMA L6-30 connectors. Weighing in at 317 kg when dry, the system’s maximum operating weight reaches 522 kg. The dielectric fluid charge is about 128 L (by volume). Key components include a condenser, variable speed coolant pump, and a microchannel radiator combined with two variable speed axial fans. The condenser consists of both internally (for the coolant flow) and externally enhanced copper tubes (for dielectric vapor condensation). The coolant consists of 5 wt% propylene glycol in water, which it is known as PG05. The tank operates as follows. As heat is generated by the IT load in the main tank, fluid boils and vapor rise and condenses back to liquid when in contact with the condenser tubes. The coolant (PG05) circulating flow will remove the heat through the radiator before returning to the condenser. The fan speed can be fixed or controlled to satisfy a given condenser coolant inlet temperature (𝑇 ). The 𝐶𝑁𝐷 𝑤,𝑖 coolant pump speed can also be fixed or controlled depending on the coolant temperature difference across the condenser. The pressure inside the tank is measured by a gauge pressure sensor and maintained within +/- 2.1 kPa, which means the fluid is always boiling near the local atmospheric pressure and that its bulk temperature is kept at saturated boiling conditions.
